Lessons.Title: How Well Can You Measure?
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Use square measurements to compare potentially proportional relationships, taking account of realistic measurement error. Original first-party teaching aligned to https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/3/1/preparation.html (OUR/IM 2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 source lineage; publisher artworks and assessments not reproduced).

For squares, diagonal length d equals side length times √2, and perimeter is four times side length. Thus perimeter/d is constant; area/d is not. Real ruler measurements may scatter near the ideal relationship.

KeyConcepts.Title: Square geometry
KeyConcepts.Definition: A square of side s has perimeter 4s, diagonal s√2 and area s².
KeyConcepts.Rule: The ratio perimeter/diagonal is 4/√2=2√2.
KeyConcepts.Example: At s=3, perimeter=12 and diagonal=3√2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measurement error
KeyConcepts.Definition: Measured lengths differ slightly from exact values.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Look for a trend close to a line through the origin.
KeyConcepts.Example: Perimeter/diagonal quotients may cluster around 2.83.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonproportional area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Square area grows quadratically with side or diagonal.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A/d=(s²)/(s√2)=s/√2 changes with s.

WorkedExamples.Title: Predict perimeter and diagonal
WorkedExamples.Question: A square has side 5 cm. Give its perimeter and exact diagonal.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain scatter from measurement
WorkedExamples.Question: Ruler estimates give diagonals 2.82 and 4.26 cm for squares with perimeters 8 and 12 cm. Are the quotients roughly equal?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
WorkedExamples.Check: Exact measured ratios need not agree perfectly.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject proportional area
WorkedExamples.Question: For squares of side 2 and 4, calculate area divided by diagonal.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: At side 2, area=4 and diagonal=2√2, ratio=√2.
At side 4, area=16 and diagonal=4√2, ratio=2√2.
Ratios differ, so the relationship is not proportional.
WorkedExamples.Check: Doubling side doubles diagonal but quadruples area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Demanding exact equality from ruler readings
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the graph trend and plausible measurement uncertainty.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating square area as proportional to diagonal length
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area is quadratic in side length.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare more than one square size.

SummaryPoints: Perimeter is proportional to diagonal length for squares.
Small measurement errors can cause scatter around a line.
Area is not proportional to square diagonal length.

Lessons.Title: Lots of Flags
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Scale fractional rectangle dimensions, compare different scales and calculate what fraction or percent of a flag is covered by a region. Original first-party teaching aligned to https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/4/1/preparation.html (OUR/IM 2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 source lineage; publisher artworks and assessments not reproduced).

A flag can be used to compare scale factors and percentages, with the denominator equal to the entire rectangle's area. These examples use independently created measurements, not official flag geometry.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale fractional dimensions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply both dimensions by the same factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If the factor is 3/2, multiply each side by 1.5.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 4 by 2.5 rectangle becomes 6 by 3.75.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area percentage
KeyConcepts.Definition: Percent coverage=part area/whole area×100.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use compatible area units.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 12 cm² part of 60 cm² covers 20%.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scaled-area invariance
KeyConcepts.Definition: Uniform scaling multiplies part and whole areas by k².
KeyConcepts.Rule: Coverage fraction is unchanged under the same scaling.
KeyConcepts.Example: If both areas quadruple, their ratio stays constant.

WorkedExamples.Title: Scale a flag
WorkedExamples.Question: A design is 4 cm by 2.5 cm. Create a factor-3/2 copy.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute region percent
WorkedExamples.Question: A 10 cm by 6 cm flag has a colored rectangle 4 cm by 3 cm. What percentage is colored?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check scaling percent
WorkedExamples.Question: Scale both flag and colored region by 2. What happens to coverage percent?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing lengths to find area coverage
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Percentage of area requires two-dimensional area quantities.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Expecting percent coverage to change under uniform scaling
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Both whole and part are scaled by the same squared factor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Reduce the fraction of new areas to verify.

SummaryPoints: Scale both fractional dimensions consistently.
Find percentage from region area over total area.
Uniform scaling leaves a region's percent coverage unchanged.

Lessons.Title: Interpreting Negative Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Compare signed rational numbers on number lines and interpret temperatures and elevations relative to zero. Original first-party teaching aligned to https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/5/1/preparation.html (OUR/IM 2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 source lineage; publisher artworks and assessments not reproduced).
A negative value indicates a location below a chosen reference point. Absolute value measures distance from zero, not whether the temperature or elevation is positive.

KeyConcepts.Title: Signed positions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Negative values lie below zero on a thermometer and below sea level for elevation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: On a horizontal number line negative numbers lie left of zero.
KeyConcepts.Example: −4°C is colder than −1°C.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number order
KeyConcepts.Definition: The number farther right on a horizontal number line is greater.
KeyConcepts.Rule: −2>−5 even though |−2|<|−5|.
KeyConcepts.Example: −2°C is warmer than −5°C.

KeyConcepts.Title: Absolute value
KeyConcepts.Definition: |x| is a nonnegative distance from 0.
KeyConcepts.Example: An elevation −7 m is 7 m below sea level.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare winter temperatures
WorkedExamples.Question: Which is colder, −4°C or −9°C?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Locate −9 to the left of −4 on a number line.

WorkedExamples.Title: Order elevations
WorkedExamples.Question: Order −3.5 m, 2 m and −0.5 m from lowest to highest.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
WorkedExamples.Check: Each position moves upward on a vertical reference line.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distance from zero
WorkedExamples.Question: How far is −6.25 from zero on a number line?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Remove the sign from the distance magnitude.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Signed order depends on position relative to zero.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a number line and compare from left to right.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing absolute value with elevation itself
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Absolute value is distance from zero, not signed location.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep position and distance in separate statements.

SummaryPoints: Signed numbers locate temperatures and elevations relative to zero.
The more negative of two numbers is smaller.
Absolute value gives nonnegative distance from zero.

Lessons.Title: Relationships between Quantities
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Recognize, reason about and explain predictable relationships that are not proportional, without requiring premature equation-solving. Original first-party teaching aligned to https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/6/1/preparation.html (OUR/IM 2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 source lineage; publisher artworks and assessments not reproduced).

This introductory source lesson expressly studies predictable nonproportional situations and allows tables, diagrams or verbal reasoning. A generic proportional-rate Practice family would test the wrong target.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonproportional relationship
KeyConcepts.Definition: A predictable rule may have a nonzero starting amount.
KeyConcepts.Rule: y=b+kx with b≠0 cannot be written y=kx.
KeyConcepts.Example: A $7 base fee plus $3 per visitor is not proportional.

KeyConcepts.Title: Recognizing patterns
KeyConcepts.Definition: Differences can remain constant even while ratios change.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare differences and quotients separately.
KeyConcepts.Example: Costs $10 for 1 visitor and $13 for 2 have ratios 10 and 6.5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Explain without algebra
KeyConcepts.Definition: Tables, diagrams or words can justify a relationship.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain what changes and what stays fixed.
KeyConcepts.Example: Each visitor adds $3, while every group starts at $7.

WorkedExamples.Title: Describe a park entry policy
WorkedExamples.Question: A park charges a $7 vehicle fee plus $3 per passenger. What do 2 and 4 passengers cost?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Explain that the fixed $7 amount remains unchanged.
WorkedExamples.Check: The cost difference for two extra passengers is $6.

WorkedExamples.Title: Show not proportional
WorkedExamples.Question: For 2 people the park costs $13, and for 4 people it costs $19. Is cost proportional to passenger count?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Different quotients mean no constant of proportionality.
WorkedExamples.Check: A fixed fee prevents a line through zero.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reason using a tape description
WorkedExamples.Question: A box contains 5 free tokens plus 4 for each visit. How many after 3 visits?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Represent 5 as a fixed starting segment.
WorkedExamples.Check: The starting 5 stays even for zero visits.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forcing every constant-difference table into y=kx
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Constant differences can describe affine, not proportional, relations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check output at zero and compare y/x.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Demanding symbolic equations in this introductory source task
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source permits reasoning with words and diagrams.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Accept mathematically justified diagrams, tables or explanations with teacher review.

SummaryPoints: Predictable does not always mean proportional.
Look for a fixed starting amount and changing ratios.
Use words, tables or diagrams to justify a nonproportional rule.

Lessons.Title: Relationships of Angles
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Use degree measure, adjacent-angle addition, straight angles and full-turn angles to find missing measures. Original first-party teaching aligned to https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/7/1/preparation.html (OUR/IM 2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 source lineage; publisher artworks and assessments not reproduced).
A right angle is 90°, a straight angle 180° and a full turn 360°. This source lesson introduces hands-on composition and reasoning, with group justification rather than only numeric arithmetic.

KeyConcepts.Title: Adjacent angles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adjacent angles share a vertex and one side without overlapping interiors.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Their measures add to the combined angle.
KeyConcepts.Example: 30° and 60° fill a 90° right angle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Straight and full turns
KeyConcepts.Definition: A straight angle is 180°; a full revolution is 360°.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use 180 or 360 as total depending on the geometry.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 125° angle on a straight line leaves 55°.

KeyConcepts.Title: Degrees
KeyConcepts.Definition: Angles measure turning, not side length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The same angle can have arbitrarily long rays.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 60° angle remains 60° if rays are extended.

WorkedExamples.Title: Complete a straight angle
WorkedExamples.Question: Adjacent angles on a straight line measure 125° and x°. Find x.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.

WorkedExamples.Title: Complete a full turn
WorkedExamples.Question: Three angles around a point measure 110°, 95° and x°. Find x.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: The total around a point is 360°.

WorkedExamples.Title: Distinguish size and drawing
WorkedExamples.Question: Two rays form a 45° angle. They are extended to double their length. What is their new angle?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Ray length does not change either direction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding angle lengths instead of measures
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Angle size does not depend on ray lengths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the measured turns in degrees.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using 360° for adjacent angles on a straight line
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A straight angle is half a full turn.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify whether the diagram shows a line or complete revolution.

SummaryPoints: Adjacent angle measures add.
Use 90°, 180° and 360° appropriately.
Angle measure depends on direction, not segment length.

Lessons.Title: Mystery Bags
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Predict outcomes using repeated trials and compare evidence about likelihood, distinguishing observations from certainty. Original first-party teaching aligned to https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/8/1/preparation.html (OUR/IM 2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 source lineage; publisher artworks and assessments not reproduced).
This source introduction uses concealed bags of colored objects and repeated experimental draws. Student predictions and arguments are teacher-reviewed; no single experimental outcome is guaranteed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Experimental frequency
KeyConcepts.Definition: Observed occurrence counts estimate likelihood.
KeyConcepts.Rule: relative frequency=successful trials/total trials.
KeyConcepts.Example: 15 blue picks in 20 draws gives 75% observed blue.

KeyConcepts.Title: Comparing experiments
KeyConcepts.Definition: More favorable outcomes in observed trials may support a likelihood prediction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare rates with equal or unequal trial counts correctly.

KeyConcepts.Title: Uncertainty
KeyConcepts.Definition: Past draws provide evidence but cannot guarantee the next independent random draw.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Report an estimated probability, not a certainty.
KeyConcepts.Example: A bag can still yield red after many blue draws.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate likelihood
WorkedExamples.Question: In 20 trials from an unknown bag, a blue cube appears 15 times. Estimate the blue rate.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Write 75% as the observed relative frequency.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is experimental evidence, not a guarantee.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare bags
WorkedExamples.Question: In 20 trials, bag A shows 12 green draws and bag B shows 8 green draws. Which is estimated more likely to yield green?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Bag A by observed relative frequency.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate a prediction
WorkedExamples.Question: A learner observes 9 blue outcomes among 10 trials and predicts that the 11th must be blue. Is that conclusion justified?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Recognize an estimated likelihood below certainty.
Explain that another color remains possible.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No: the observation supports a high likelihood, not certainty.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the reasoning about randomness.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating relative frequency as a guaranteed next result
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use words such as 'estimated' and 'more likely'.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing only raw successful counts with unequal trials
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Different sample sizes require comparable rates.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Divide by the number of trials before comparing.

SummaryPoints: Use repeated trials to estimate likelihood.
Compare relative frequencies rather than raw counts.
Random outcomes remain uncertain; justify predictions with evidence.

Lessons.Title: Planning Recipes
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Scale ingredient and nutritional information per serving and justify a recipe meeting specified nutrient thresholds. Original first-party teaching aligned to https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/9/1/preparation.html (OUR/IM 2017–2019 CC BY 4.0 source lineage; publisher artworks and assessments not reproduced).

This optional open-ended source lesson asks learners to select or invent a recipe and defend their nutrition calculations. The numeric worked examples support arithmetic; the authentic recipe and justification require teacher assessment.

KeyConcepts.Title: Per-serving proportion
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide the recipe total by the number of servings.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Per-serving nutrient=recipe total/servings.
KeyConcepts.Example: 600 kcal across 4 servings gives 150 kcal each.

KeyConcepts.Title: Serving rescale
KeyConcepts.Definition: To change serving count, scale ingredient amounts with one consistent factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: New amount=old amount×new servings/old servings.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four servings to six means factor 1.5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constraint checking
KeyConcepts.Definition: A recipe meets a stated threshold only if its computed per-serving value satisfies the bound.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Specify numerical nutrition limits and units.
KeyConcepts.Example: If a task says at most 200 kcal, 180 qualifies.

WorkedExamples.Title: Calories per serving
WorkedExamples.Question: A recipe has 720 kcal and makes 6 equal servings. Find kcal per serving.
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: Divide total calories by serving count.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rescale ingredients
WorkedExamples.Question: A four-serving recipe uses 300 g of rice. How much is needed for six equal servings?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.

WorkedExamples.Title: Review a nutrition requirement
WorkedExamples.Question: A fictional recipe provides 900 kcal for five servings. The task defines 'low calorie' as at most 200 kcal per serving. Does this recipe meet that task-specific criterion?
WorkedExamples.Method: Show the relevant mathematical reasoning with units or justified conditions; verify the result.
Steps: State that the threshold is a classroom assumption, not a universal health definition.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes under the specified classroom threshold.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the full invented recipe, source data and reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying a nutrition threshold without defining it
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Criteria differ by task, food label and jurisdiction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the exact threshold supplied by the assignment; do not invent regulatory claims.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing one ingredient by the wrong number of portions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: All recipe totals must use the same serving basis.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check serving count and units across all ingredients.

SummaryPoints: Convert recipe totals to per-serving values.
Scale every ingredient consistently when changing servings.
Human review is required for an invented recipe and its justification.
